lessonTitle: Immunisation Programmes: Herd Immunity, Live Vaccine Contraindications and Safety Monitoring

blocks.text: A 6-month-old baby, too young for her first measles vaccine, is admitted with measles after a single unvaccinated child visited her nursery. She cannot be protected by her own immune system, yet in communities with very high vaccine coverage she would almost never have met the virus. Protection that belongs to a population rather than an individual is the central idea of an immunisation programme.

blocks.title: Herd immunity
blocks.text: Herd (population) immunity is the indirect protection of susceptible individuals that occurs when a large enough proportion of the population is immune, so that each infectious person meets too few susceptible people to sustain transmission. It protects those who cannot be vaccinated, such as infants and immunosuppressed patients.

blocks.markdown: The **basic reproduction number, R0**, is the average number of secondary cases produced by one infectious person in a **fully susceptible** population. If R0 is greater than 1, an outbreak can grow; if it is below 1, it fades. Immunity in a fraction of the population reduces the number of new infections each case produces. The **effective reproduction number** is R0 multiplied by the fraction still susceptible. Transmission is no longer self-sustaining when this effective number falls to 1 or below.

blocks.caption: Herd immunity threshold: p_c is the minimum proportion immune needed to interrupt sustained transmission (assumes random mixing and a homogeneous population)

blocks.title: Deriving the threshold
blocks.prompt: Show why the proportion immune must exceed 1 - 1/R0 to prevent outbreaks, then calculate it for R0 = 5.

steps.text: If a fraction p is immune, each case meets susceptibles only in a fraction (1 - p) of contacts, so the effective reproduction number is R0 x (1 - p).
Spread stops when R0 x (1 - p) is at most 1, so (1 - p) is at most 1/R0 and p is at least 1 - 1/R0.

blocks.answer: At least 80% of the population must be immune when R0 = 5.

blocks.markdown: **Why measles needs very high coverage.** Measles has one of the highest R0 values of any infection (often quoted between about 12 and 18), so more than about 90-95% of the population must be immune. **Imperfect vaccines** require higher coverage: if the vaccine protects a fraction **E** (effectiveness) of those who receive it, the coverage needed is the threshold divided by E. In practice coverage is uneven, and **clusters of unvaccinated people** allow outbreaks even when the national average seems high.

blocks.caption: E: vaccine effectiveness as a proportion

blocks.title: Coverage with an imperfect vaccine
blocks.prompt: A pathogen has R0 = 6 and the vaccine is 90% effective. What coverage is needed?

steps.text: Divide by E = 0.90: 0.833 / 0.90 = 0.926, or about 92.6% coverage.

blocks.answer: About 92.6% of the population must be vaccinated.

blocks.markdown: **Contraindications to live vaccines.** Live attenuated vaccines (for example measles-mumps-rubella, varicella, BCG, yellow fever, oral rotavirus) contain replicating, weakened organisms. They are generally **contraindicated** in: **severe immunosuppression** (for example high-dose corticosteroids, chemotherapy, advanced HIV infection with a low CD4 count, some biological therapies, after transplantation) because the weakened organism may cause disease; **pregnancy** (avoided because of a theoretical risk to the fetus); and a previous **anaphylactic reaction** to a vaccine component. Two live injectable vaccines should be given on the same day or separated by about four weeks. Inactivated, subunit and toxoid vaccines cannot replicate and are generally safe in immunosuppressed people, although the response may be reduced. Always check current national guidance, which varies.

blocks.caption: Live vaccines: when to avoid
rows: Severe immunodeficiency (chemotherapy, advanced HIV, transplant, high-dose steroids)
Vaccine strain may replicate uncontrollably and cause disease
Theoretical risk to the fetus; vaccinate before or after pregnancy
Previous anaphylaxis to a vaccine component

blocks.markdown: **Safety monitoring after licensing.** Pre-licensure trials involve thousands of participants and cannot detect **rare** adverse events (for example one in several hundred thousand). **Post-marketing surveillance (pharmacovigilance)** continues after licensing. **Passive surveillance** relies on clinicians and the public reporting suspected **adverse events following immunisation (AEFI)** through national systems; it is quick and sensitive to unexpected signals but cannot prove cause because reports lack a denominator and a comparison group. **Active surveillance** studies linked population databases of vaccination and health records, using methods such as the **self-controlled case series** and cohort comparisons, to test whether an event is more common after vaccination than expected by chance. Detected signals are assessed for **causality** (timing, biological plausibility, alternative causes) and result in label changes, restricted use or withdrawal where appropriate. An event that follows vaccination is not necessarily caused by it.

blocks.title: Population protection is not uniform
blocks.text: A high national average can hide local pockets of low coverage where transmission persists. Programmes track coverage by area and group, not just overall.

blocks.title: Assumptions behind the formula
blocks.text: The threshold assumes homogeneous mixing and a perfect, life-long vaccine unless corrected for effectiveness. Real populations are structured and immunity may wane, so these numbers are estimates.

points: Herd immunity protects non-immune people when enough of the population is immune; the threshold depends on R0.
Live vaccines are contraindicated in severe immunosuppression, pregnancy and after anaphylaxis to a component.
Safety after licensing relies on passive reporting and active surveillance of linked data, with causality assessment.

questions.stem: What does the basic reproduction number R0 measure?

options.text: The average number of secondary cases from one infectious person in a fully susceptible population
The proportion of the population that is vaccinated
The proportion of cases that die
The number of days an infected person is contagious

questions.correctOptionText: The average number of secondary cases from one infectious person in a fully susceptible population

distractorRationale.d: That is infectious period, one component of R0.

questions.explanation: R0 describes transmissibility in a population with no immunity. The higher it is, the greater the immune proportion needed to stop spread.

questions.stem: Why does measles require a higher vaccination coverage for herd immunity than a pathogen with a lower R0?

options.text: A higher R0 means each case infects more people, so a greater proportion must be immune to reduce the effective reproduction number to 1 or below
Measles vaccine is less effective than all others
Measles cannot be prevented by vaccination
Herd immunity is not relevant for measles

questions.correctOptionText: A higher R0 means each case infects more people, so a greater proportion must be immune to reduce the effective reproduction number to 1 or below

distractorRationale.b: Measles vaccine is highly effective; the threshold is high because of R0.
distractorRationale.d: Herd immunity is very relevant to measles.

questions.explanation: The threshold 1 - 1/R0 rises steeply as R0 increases. With R0 in the range of 12 to 18 the threshold exceeds 90%.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is 12 weeks pregnant and has no immunity to rubella on antenatal testing. Which approach is appropriate regarding MMR vaccine?

options.text: Avoid the live vaccine in pregnancy and vaccinate after delivery
Give it now because live vaccines are always safe in pregnancy
Give it only if she has a low CD4 count
Give a double dose to compensate

questions.correctOptionText: Avoid the live vaccine in pregnancy and vaccinate after delivery

distractorRationale.b: Live vaccines are avoided in pregnancy because of theoretical fetal risk.
distractorRationale.c: CD4 count is irrelevant and a low count is itself a contraindication.
distractorRationale.d: Doubling the dose is not a recognised practice.

questions.explanation: MMR contains live attenuated virus, so it is avoided in pregnancy because of a theoretical risk to the fetus. Vaccination is offered postpartum to protect future pregnancies.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man is about to start chemotherapy that will cause profound immunosuppression. Which vaccine is contraindicated?

options.text: A live attenuated yellow fever vaccine
An inactivated influenza vaccine
A tetanus toxoid vaccine
A pneumococcal conjugate vaccine

questions.correctOptionText: A live attenuated yellow fever vaccine

distractorRationale.a: Correct: live vaccines are contraindicated in severe immunosuppression.
distractorRationale.b: Inactivated vaccines are safe, though response may be reduced.

questions.explanation: A weakened live organism may replicate uncontrollably in a person without effective immune control. Inactivated, toxoid and conjugate vaccines cannot replicate and are used.

questions.stem: A new vaccine has been licensed after trials of 30 000 participants. Which approach is best able to detect an adverse event occurring in about one in 500 000 recipients?

options.text: Post-licensing surveillance including spontaneous reporting and linked population database studies
Repeating the pre-licensure trial with the same sample size
Relying only on the manufacturer's laboratory data
Waiting for the vaccine to be withdrawn

questions.correctOptionText: Post-licensing surveillance including spontaneous reporting and linked population database studies

distractorRationale.b: A trial of 30 000 will usually miss an event at this frequency.
distractorRationale.c: Laboratory data cannot reveal rare population events.

questions.explanation: Rare events need very large numbers of vaccinees to appear. Passive reporting generates signals and linked database studies test them against background rates.

questions.stem: A pathogen has a basic reproduction number R0 of 8, and the vaccine gives perfect protection. Calculate the herd immunity threshold as a percentage of the population that must be immune.
questions.explanation: Threshold = 1 - 1/R0 = 1 - 1/8 = 0.875, or 87.5%. Above this proportion immune, each case infects fewer than one other person on average.

questions.stem: A pathogen has R0 = 4, and the vaccine is 80% effective in preventing infection (E = 0.80). Using coverage = (1 - 1/R0) / E, calculate the vaccination coverage needed, as a percentage.
questions.explanation: The threshold is 1 - 1/4 = 0.75. Dividing by 0.80 gives 0.9375, or about 94% coverage. An imperfect vaccine therefore demands higher coverage than a perfect one.

questions.stem: Explain what is meant by herd immunity and how the herd immunity threshold depends on the basic reproduction number.
markingGuide: Herd immunity: indirect protection of susceptibles when enough of the population is immune to interrupt transmission
R0 is the average number of secondary cases in a fully susceptible population
Higher R0 gives a higher threshold (example calculation)
Vaccines that are less than perfect require higher coverage; assumptions include random mixing
questions.explanation: Each immune person reduces the contacts available to the infection. The threshold is reached when the effective reproduction number falls to 1.

questions.stem: Describe three situations in which a live attenuated vaccine is contraindicated, giving the reason for each, and name one vaccine type that remains safe in such patients.
markingGuide: Severe immunosuppression (chemotherapy, advanced HIV, high-dose steroids, transplant): vaccine organism may replicate and cause disease
Pregnancy: theoretical risk to the fetus
Previous anaphylaxis to a vaccine component: risk of severe allergic reaction
Inactivated, subunit, toxoid or conjugate vaccines cannot replicate and are generally safe, though response may be reduced
questions.explanation: Live vaccines replicate, which is the source of their strong immunity and of the risk in those who cannot control the organism. Non-replicating vaccines avoid this risk.

questions.stem: Describe how the safety of a vaccine is monitored after licensing, and explain why a single report of an adverse event after vaccination does not prove the vaccine caused it.
markingGuide: Pre-licensure trials too small to detect rare events
Passive surveillance: spontaneous AEFI reports to national systems generate signals
Active surveillance: linked databases, cohort and self-controlled case series studies compare observed with expected rates
Causality assessment: timing, plausibility, alternative explanations
Reports lack a denominator and comparison group; events may be coincidental because many illnesses occur by chance after vaccination
Outcomes: label changes, restrictions or withdrawal
questions.explanation: Reporting systems detect signals but cannot establish cause. Comparing observed with expected rates in a defined population is needed to test whether an association is real.
